client.name: Failaka Foods Trading Co.
client.profile: Client for 4 years. Clean account conduct, growing steadily. Imports frozen foods and distributes to co-ops and restaurants.

request: "We found a new supplier in Brazil with great prices, but they won't ship without secure payment — and I'm not wiring KD 250,000 in advance to someone I've never met. What can the bank do?"

ratios.label: Current ratio
ratios.hint: Short-term assets comfortably cover short-term liabilities — liquidity is healthy.

ratios.label: Leverage (Debt / Equity)
ratios.hint: Low debt — the company is not over-borrowed.

ratios.label: Inventory days
ratios.hint: Stock sells in about two months.

decisions.prompt: The supplier wants assured payment on shipment; the client refuses to prepay. What do you offer?

options.label: Sight Letter of Credit — KD 250,000
options.detail: Bank pays the supplier when compliant shipping documents are presented.
options.feedback: Exactly right. A sight LC protects both sides: the supplier is sure of payment, and the client's money only moves against documents proving the goods were shipped as agreed.

options.label: Overdraft KD 250,000 so he can wire the money in advance
options.feedback: This funds a blind prepayment to an unknown supplier — if the goods never ship, the money is gone and the bank financed the loss. The LC exists precisely to avoid this.

options.label: Usance LC (Acceptance) — 180 days
options.feedback: A usance LC defers payment — but this supplier insists on payment at shipment, so they will reject these terms and the deal stalls. Instrument family is right; the variant is wrong.

options.label: Term Loan KD 250,000 over 5 years
options.feedback: Term loans finance fixed assets repaid over years. This is a 60-day trading transaction — completely the wrong tenor and type.

decisions.prompt: What security do you take for the LC line?

options.label: 15% cash margin + personal guarantee of the partners
options.feedback: Proportionate for a healthy 4-year client: the margin gives a first-loss cushion, the PG keeps the owners committed.

options.label: 100% cash margin
options.feedback: Completely safe for the bank — but if the client had KD 250,000 idle, they would barely need us. Commercially heavy for a client of this quality; expect them to shop around.

options.label: Clean — no security
options.feedback: An unsecured trade line for a mid-sized private company leaves the bank with nothing if documents arrive and the client can't pay.

options.label: First-degree mortgage over the GM's home
options.feedback: Disproportionate for a KD 250,000 trade line on a healthy client — slow, expensive to register, and likely to push the client to a competitor.

learn: A sight LC pays the supplier only against compliant shipping documents — it replaces risky advance payments in international trade. Security should be proportionate to the client's strength.

client.name: Mubarakiya Textiles Trading
client.profile: Family business, 12 years old, buys from local wholesalers and importers. Sales peak strongly every year before Ramadan and Eid.

request: "Every year before Ramadan I need to build stock — about KD 400,000 extra for roughly three months. I repay it all once the season's sales come in. It happens every single year. What's the right way to fund this?"

ratios.label: Working capital cycle
ratios.hint: Money invested in stock comes back as cash in about 75 days — that's the natural tenor of the financing.

ratios.label: Seasonal peak need
ratios.hint: Pre-computed: peak inventory minus normal inventory. The number matches what he's asking for.

decisions.prompt: A recurring, 3-month seasonal stock build, repaid from seasonal sales. What fits?

options.label: Short Term Revolving Loan — KD 400,000, drawdowns up to 90 days
options.feedback: Textbook STRL: it funds the operating cycle, each drawdown matches the ~75–90 day cycle, he repays from season sales and redraws next year. Self-liquidating by design.

options.label: Term Loan KD 400,000 over 5 years
options.feedback: He needs the money for 3 months a year and you've lent it for 5 years — he pays interest on idle money for the other 9 months, every year. Wrong tenor for a working capital need.

options.label: Overdraft KD 400,000
options.feedback: It works — but an OD this size invites drift into permanent usage. An STRL with 90-day drawdowns imposes the discipline of repaying each season, which is exactly the rhythm of his business.

options.label: Sight LC line KD 400,000
options.feedback: He buys from local wholesalers in dinars — there's no international trade transaction here for an LC to secure.

options.label: Personal guarantee of the owner
options.feedback: Standard and proportionate for a 12-year family business with healthy ratios — keeps the owner personally committed to the seasonal repayment.

options.label: Clean, based on strong financials and track record
options.feedback: Defensible for this client — but a PG costs the client nothing and meaningfully strengthens the bank's position. Why lend clean when a PG is easy to obtain?

options.label: 100% cash margin
options.feedback: If he had KD 400,000 in spare cash he wouldn't be asking for seasonal finance. This effectively declines the deal.

options.label: Pledge over listed shares
options.feedback: He's a textile trader — he holds stock, not a share portfolio. Security should connect to what the client actually has.

learn: The Short Term Revolving Loan funds the operating cycle: draw to buy stock, repay from sales, redraw next cycle. Size it from the cycle, and match each drawdown's tenor to it.

client.name: Al Sawari Contracting Co.
client.profile: Mid-size contractor, client for 6 years. Has completed six government renovation projects on time. Currently bidding for new work.

request: "We're bidding on the Ministry of Health clinic renovation tender — contract value around KD 2,500,000. The tender requires a 2% bank guarantee with the bid, submitted by Thursday. We need it fast."

ratios.label: Execution track record
ratios.hint: Six similar projects completed — they can genuinely perform if they win. That's the key question behind any bid bond.

decisions.prompt: What does the client actually need for the tender?

options.label: Bid Bond — KD 50,000, valid per tender conditions
options.feedback: Correct. The bid bond (2% of tender value) accompanies the offer and compensates the Ministry if the bidder wins then withdraws. It's the first rung of the guarantee ladder.

options.label: Performance Bond — KD 250,000 now
options.feedback: The performance bond comes after the award, not at bidding. Issuing 10% of contract value now is premature and five times the exposure needed today.

options.label: Overdraft KD 50,000 so they deposit cash with the Ministry
options.feedback: The tender asks for a bank guarantee. A cash deposit (even if accepted) ties up the client's liquidity for months across every tender they bid — guarantees exist to avoid exactly this.

options.label: Sight LC in favour of the Ministry
options.feedback: An LC is a trade payment instrument against shipping documents. A tender requires a letter of guarantee — different instrument, different purpose.

options.label: 10% cash margin + counter-indemnity signed by the company
options.feedback: Standard structure: the counter-indemnity gives the bank recourse if the bond is called, and a modest margin reflects the client's strong track record.

options.label: Clean — strong 6-year relationship
options.feedback: Arguable for KD 50,000 on this client — but a counter-indemnity is mandatory practice on any LG, and skipping the margin sets a precedent for the much larger bonds that follow if they win.

options.label: 100% cash margin
options.feedback: Contractors bid on several tenders at once — demanding full cash cover on every bid bond would freeze their liquidity and send them to a competitor.

options.label: Real estate mortgage before issuing
options.feedback: Registering a mortgage takes weeks; the bid closes Thursday. Disproportionate and impossible in the timeframe.

plantedError.prompt: Operations flags the file before issuing the guarantee. Review the checklist — is anything wrong?
exhibit: Tender documents — MOH clinic renovation, bid bond KD 50,000, validity 90 days
Trade license No. 88412 — valid until 9 April 2026
Board resolution authorising bank facilities — signed and on file
Authorised signatory list — matches specimen cards

options.label: The trade license on file expired two months ago
options.feedback: Caught it. Issuing a guarantee for a company whose trade license has lapsed is a compliance breach — get the renewed license before anything is issued.

options.label: The tender documents shouldn't be in the file
options.feedback: Tender documents are exactly what we need — they define the required bond amount, wording and validity.

options.label: Nothing — the file is complete, issue the bond
options.feedback: Look again at the trade license dates. It expired two months ago — a lapsed license must be renewed before issuance.

learn: The guarantee ladder follows the project: Bid Bond at tender → Performance Bond and APG at award → Retention Bond at completion. Behind every bond, the real question is: can this client perform?

client.name: Shamal Steel Industries
client.profile: Specialist steel contractor, client for 3 years. Just received an award letter from the Ministry of Electricity & Water.

request: "Good news — we won the KD 1,800,000 substation steelworks contract! The Ministry requires a 10% performance bond before signing, and they're offering a 15% advance payment if we provide a guarantee for it. We want both, and the advance would really help us mobilise."

ratios.label: Contract / revenue
ratios.hint: A big job for them, but within capacity given their track record on similar work.

options.label: Performance Bond KD 180,000 + APG KD 270,000, with the advance paid into their account with us
options.feedback: Complete and controlled: the PB satisfies the Ministry, the APG unlocks KD 270,000 of free mobilisation money, and routing the advance through the bank lets you see it spent on the project — not elsewhere.

options.label: Performance Bond only — skip the advance, less exposure for us
options.feedback: You just declined KD 270,000 of interest-free funding for your client's mobilisation. They'll either strain their own cash or borrow it — at interest — possibly from another bank.

options.label: Overdraft KD 450,000 to cover both needs in cash
options.feedback: The Ministry requires guarantees, not cash, and an OD replaces a free advance with interest-bearing debt. Wrong instruments entirely.

options.label: APG only — the advance matters more than the bond
options.feedback: No performance bond means no signed contract — the Ministry requires it before signature. Without the contract there is no advance to guarantee either.

decisions.prompt: How do you protect the bank on KD 450,000 of guarantees?

options.label: Assignment of contract proceeds + advance routed through the bank + 10% cash margin
options.feedback: The strongest package: every Ministry payment flows through us, we watch the advance being used for mobilisation, and the margin cushions a call. The repayment source itself is the security.

options.label: Personal guarantees of the partners only
options.feedback: Keeps the partners committed, but misses the natural security sitting right there: the Ministry's own payments. Always take the assignment of proceeds on contracting deals.

options.label: 100% cash margin on both bonds
options.feedback: KD 450,000 of blocked cash would consume the advance and more — the client would be worse off than before winning the contract.

options.label: Clean — it's a government contract, nothing can go wrong
options.feedback: The employer is solid; the risk is the contractor failing to perform. If the project stalls, both bonds get called and the bank has nothing.

learn: After award: Performance Bond to sign, APG to unlock the advance. Route the advance through the bank and take an assignment of contract proceeds — the contract payments are the natural security.

client.name: Sidra Medical Supplies
client.profile: Distributes medical consumables to clinics and pharmacies. Client for 5 years, profitable every year.

request: "Our delivery fleet is falling apart — we need six new vans, about KD 120,000 total. Just put it on an overdraft, that's easiest, right?"

ratios.label: DSCR at 4-year tenor
ratios.hint: Pre-computed: yearly cash flow covers the proposed instalments 1.8 times over. Comfortable.

decisions.prompt: Vans are a fixed asset lasting ~5 years. The client asked for an overdraft. What do you actually book?

options.label: Term Loan KD 120,000 over 4 years, monthly instalments
options.feedback: Right structure: tenor inside the vans' useful life, instalments paid from the cash flow the fleet generates, and DSCR of 1.8x says it's comfortably affordable.

options.label: Overdraft KD 120,000 — as she asked
options.feedback: Classic maturity mismatch: a 5-year asset sitting permanently on a facility designed for daily swings. The OD will be stuck at its limit for years, and the first cash squeeze becomes a crisis. 'The client asked for it' is not a structure.

options.label: Short Term Revolving Loan KD 120,000
options.feedback: The STRL funds inventory and receivables that convert back to cash each cycle. Vans don't convert to cash — this drawdown would never revolve.

options.label: Sight LC for the van purchase
options.feedback: The vans are bought from a local dealer in dinars — there's no cross-border trade transaction to secure. And an LC still leaves the question: what funds the payment?

options.label: Lien over the vans + personal guarantee of the CEO
options.feedback: The financed asset secures its own loan, and the PG keeps the owner committed. Proportionate and standard.

options.label: Clean — small loan, strong client
options.feedback: Survivable for KD 120,000 on a 5-year client — but the lien over the vans costs nothing to ask for. Take the easy security.

options.label: 100% cash margin
options.feedback: Blocking KD 120,000 to lend KD 120,000 — she'd rightly ask what the loan is for.

options.label: Pledge over listed shares
options.feedback: She runs a distribution company, not a portfolio. The natural security is the asset being financed — the vans.

plantedError.prompt: Documentation review before signing the facility agreement. Anything wrong with the file?
exhibit: Supplier quotation — 6 delivery vans, total KD 120,000
Audited financial statements — last 3 years on file
Authorised signatory list & specimen signatures — on file
Facility agreement — prepared and ready for signing

options.label: There is no board resolution authorising the borrowing
options.feedback: Correct. Without a valid resolution authorising the company to borrow and naming who signs, the facility agreement may be unenforceable. Never sign without it.

options.label: The supplier quotation should not be in the credit file
options.feedback: The quotation is needed — it evidences what we're financing and the amount.

options.label: Nothing — proceed to signing
options.feedback: Check the corporate authorisations: there's no board resolution to borrow in the file. That's a blocking gap.

learn: Match the financing to the asset: fixed assets take term loans with tenors inside the asset's life, repaid by the cash flow it generates. DSCR above ~1.2x is the affordability test — and it's computed for you in the pack.

client.name: Gulf Crescent Electronics
client.profile: Client for 7 years, excellent account conduct. Sells to both walk-in customers and corporate accounts.

request: "Our corporate customers pay on the 25th but our suppliers debit us on the 10th. Two weeks every month we're stretched — maybe KD 60,000 at the worst point — then it clears. Can we get some kind of loan?"

figures.label: Account turnover with us
figures.value: KD 220,000 / month, always returns to credit

ratios.label: Account conduct
ratios.hint: The account swings into and out of credit every month — that's the natural shape of an overdraft user.

decisions.prompt: A two-week timing gap, every month, that always self-corrects. What fits?

options.label: Overdraft — KD 75,000 limit
options.feedback: The textbook overdraft case: short-lived swings that clear naturally. Interest only on days used, and his account history shows it will swing back into credit every month — which is your monitoring signal too.

options.label: Short Term Revolving Loan KD 75,000
options.feedback: Workable, but heavier than needed — fixed drawdowns and maturities for a gap that lasts two weeks. The OD's daily flexibility fits this pattern better.

options.label: Short-Term Loan KD 75,000, 6-month bullet
options.feedback: A lump sum for six months to cover a two-week monthly wobble — he pays interest on money he doesn't need for most of the period.

options.label: Term Loan KD 75,000 over 3 years
options.feedback: Three years of debt for a recurring two-week timing gap — the most expensive and least flexible answer possible.

options.label: Personal guarantee of the partners
options.feedback: Proportionate for a small, self-correcting line on a 7-year client with excellent conduct.

options.label: Clean — based on 7 years of excellent conduct
options.feedback: Defensible here — conduct is genuinely strong and the amount is modest. Still, a PG is a costless ask that protects the bank if things ever change.

options.label: Real estate mortgage
options.feedback: Weeks of registration and legal cost for a KD 75,000 swing line. The client will laugh, then leave.

options.label: 100% cash margin
options.feedback: A fully cash-collateralised overdraft is a contradiction — if he had the cash parked, there would be no gap to fund.

learn: Overdrafts suit short-lived, self-correcting swings — the account should return to credit regularly. An OD stuck at its limit is no longer an OD; it's a misclassified loan.

client.name: Desert Rose Hospitality Group
client.profile: Runs nine cafés and two restaurants. Client for 2 years, expanding steadily. Imports specialty coffee and foodstuffs from Italy.

request: "Our Italian supplier offered us 90-day payment terms — but only if a bank stands behind the payment. Our stock sells through in about 70 days, so we'd collect from customers before we even pay them. How do we set this up?"

ratios.label: Inventory days
ratios.hint: Stock converts to cash in 70 days — inside the 90-day terms the supplier is offering. The trade finances itself.

decisions.prompt: Deferred payment to an overseas supplier, backed by the bank. What's the instrument?

options.label: Usance LC (Acceptance) — 90 days, line of KD 200,000
options.feedback: Exactly it. The bank accepts the obligation to pay at 90 days; her stock sells in 70, so customer cash arrives before the LC falls due. Self-liquidating trade finance at its cleanest.

options.label: Sight LC — KD 200,000
options.feedback: Safe and workable — but it throws away the 90 days of free supplier credit she just negotiated, and she'd need other funding to bridge the 70-day stock cycle. Why pay at shipment when the supplier offered terms?

options.label: Overdraft KD 200,000 to pay the supplier directly
options.feedback: Replaces free supplier credit with interest-bearing bank debt, and gives up the LC's document control on cross-border shipments.

options.label: Term Loan KD 200,000 over 5 years
options.feedback: Five-year debt for coffee that sells in 70 days. Wrong instrument, wrong tenor, wrong everything.

decisions.prompt: Security for the usance LC line?

options.label: 10% cash margin + personal guarantee
options.feedback: Proportionate: a modest first-loss cushion plus owner commitment, on a line whose own trade cycle repays it.

options.label: Clean line
options.feedback: A 2-year relationship is still young for clean trade lines — a small margin and PG cost the client little and protect the bank meaningfully.

options.label: 100% cash margin
options.feedback: Full cash cover defeats the purpose of the supplier's credit terms — the client funds everything anyway.

options.label: Mortgage over one of the restaurant premises
options.feedback: Heavy, slow security for a self-liquidating 90-day trade line. Keep mortgages for term exposure.

learn: Usance LC (Acceptance) = LC with deferred payment. When the usance period covers the inventory turnover, the trade finances itself: stock sells before the payment falls due.

client.name: Al-Dhow Marine Services
client.profile: Provides maintenance and logistics services to the public port authority. Client for 5 years. Work is steady; payment is slow.

request: "The port authority always pays — but in 120 days, sometimes more. Meanwhile I have salaries every month. Right now I'm sitting on KD 350,000 of approved, certified invoices. Can the bank turn those into cash?"

ratios.label: Receivable days
ratios.hint: The problem in one number: work done, cash four months away.

ratios.label: Debtor quality
ratios.hint: In discounting, the debtor's quality matters more than the client's. This debtor is as strong as they come.

decisions.prompt: Strong receivables, slow payer, cash needed now. What's the facility?

options.label: Invoice Discounting line KD 300,000 — advance ~80% against approved invoices, with recourse
options.feedback: Purpose-built for this: the bank advances against certified government invoices and collects when the authority pays. The margin (advancing 80%, not 100%) absorbs deductions and delays.

options.label: Short Term Revolving Loan KD 300,000
options.feedback: It funds the same gap, but as general-purpose borrowing — it doesn't tie the financing to the specific strong invoices, which is where the credit strength of this deal actually lives.

options.label: Overdraft KD 300,000
options.feedback: A 120-day structural collection lag is not a short-lived swing — this OD would sit fully drawn for months at a time.

options.label: Term Loan KD 300,000 over 5 years
options.feedback: There's no fixed asset and no 5-year need — the cash arrives in 120 days. Wrong instrument.

options.label: Assignment of the discounted receivables, with the port authority notified to pay the bank directly
options.feedback: The essential structure: the debtor pays the bank, not the client. Without notification, collections pass through the client's hands — and can go elsewhere.

options.label: Personal guarantee of the owner only
options.feedback: Recourse to Bader helps, but the deal's whole strength is the government receivable — if you don't take the assignment, you've left the best security on the table.

options.label: Clean — the government always pays
options.feedback: The government pays the client. Without an assignment, nothing makes that money reach the bank.

options.label: Pledge over the company's workboats
options.feedback: Illiquid, hard-to-value security when a far better one exists: the receivables themselves.

facilitySummary: Invoice Discounting line KD 300,000 (port authority invoices)

plantedError.prompt: Operations checks the first batch of invoices submitted for discounting. Anything wrong?
exhibit: Batch of 9 invoices submitted for discounting — total KD 350,000
7 invoices — port authority certification stamp present
Notification letter — acknowledged by the port authority

options.label: Two invoices have no certification stamp from the port authority
options.feedback: Correct. Only certified/approved invoices are eligible — an uncertified invoice may be disputed, leaving the bank advancing against air. Return them for certification.

options.label: The invoices show the client's logo, which is unprofessional
options.feedback: The client's own invoices naturally carry their logo — that's not an issue.

options.label: Nothing — advance against the full batch
options.feedback: Check the certification stamps: two invoices were never approved by the debtor. Those are not eligible.

learn: Discounting turns strong receivables into immediate cash. The debtor's quality is the real credit; the assignment with debtor notification is the real security; and only certified invoices count.
